A warm day lowers the amount of dissolved CO₂ in leaf cells while O₂ builds up (because warm leaves hold relatively less CO₂ and the stomata tend to close to conserve water). This makes O₂ compete more strongly with CO₂ for RuBisCO’s active site. When RuBisCO fixes O₂ instead of CO₂, the plant undergoes photorespiration, which consumes ATP and releases CO₂ without producing sugar—i.e., it wastes energy. [3][5]
reference_answer: Higher temperature makes oxygen compete with carbon dioxide at RuBisCO, which increases photorespiration.

answer: A warm day raises the chance that RuBisCO will bind oxygen instead of carbon dioxide. Heat makes leaves hold relatively less dissolved CO₂ while oxygen builds up, and the plants often close their stomata to conserve water, which further lowers internal CO₂ and raises O₂ levels. Under these conditions RuBisCO catalyzes photorespiration, producing the toxic phosphoglycolate and wasting energy that could have been used for carbon fixation[1]. Because RuBisCO evolved when atmospheric O₂ was low, it handles O₂ poorly, so the increased O₂ competition on hot days makes the enzyme more likely to waste energy[2].
reference_answer: Higher temperature makes oxygen compete with carbon dioxide at RuBisCO, which increases photorespiration.
